source.title: Rethinking Bayesian Optimization for Co-Optimizing LLM Training Configurations
source.authors: Zhi-Liang Chen; A. Leong; Yong-Ong Shao; Apivich Hemachandra; G. Lau; Chuan-Sheng Foo; Zhengyuan Liu; Nancy F. Chen; B. Low

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: JoBS uses a scaling-law-inspired predictor to extrapolate fine-tuning performance from short runs, but it does not test the claimed pretraining loss laws or their exponents and allocations.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses classical scaling-law formulas and reports fine-tuning performance prediction results. Those results concern a neural-network predictor across training configurations, not power-law fits of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute. No claim version is directly tested. The related predictor results are recorded as none-version rows.
record.test_reason: The paper uses a 'scaling-law-inspired' neural-network predictor to estimate final fine-tuning accuracy from the first 100 of 1000 steps. It reports only that predictor's accuracy and the BO method's performance. It never fits or checks a power law in parameters, tokens or compute, any extrapolation across scale, any compute-optimal allocation, or any shape effect. Its remark that symbolic scaling laws do not transfer across training configurations is an argument for its design choice, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Two points should be added. The authors' main conclusion is that JoBS, BO with a learned early-training predictor, outperforms independent data/model optimization and multi-fidelity BO baselines across six tasks, with a derived optimal budget split (N≈30). They also say symbolic scaling laws, being tied to fixed configurations, cannot be applied in their setting.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a neural-network predictor inspired by scaling-law extrapolation, trained on short-run fine-tuning observations and configuration inputs; it does not fit the original power-law loss equations.
record.method_sensitivity: Predictor accuracy improves with more initial full training runs N; the paper also reports that performance trajectories differ across training configurations, including declining performance for a suboptimal configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: Within LoRA fine-tuning of an 8B model, downstream accuracy can fall as training steps increase under a poor data mixture. A neural predictor using steps 25–100 plus the configuration estimates step-1000 accuracy, and its error shrinks as the number of training runs N grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Final fine-tuning performance across data/model configurations can be predicted from early-training observations with a learned non-symbolic predictor. Fixed-configuration scaling formulas do not capture non-monotone trajectories.

record.problems: The predictor-error results are described qualitatively in the text and shown in figures without numerical values in the provided text. The paper does not test the power-law relations in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were extracted: the remaining reported comparisons concern JoBS optimization performance against baselines, not power-law scaling or its predictor-error behavior.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-to-large-run extrapolation. The predictor extrapolates over training steps at fixed model size, using a neural net rather than a power law.
No fixed-parameter-count architecture-shape comparison. LoRA configuration changes accuracy by over 10%, but these are not depth/width choices at matched size.
Fine-tuning is studied, but no power-law form is fitted in fine-tuning.
Downstream accuracy is not related to model scale or to pretraining loss. Qwen3-14B/32B appear only as settings for evaluating the method.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not an original source. 'Scaling-law-inspired' is a label only: the predictor is a 3-layer MLP with no power-law form. The code URLs in the abstract and the checklist differ, as the record notes. The venue and date (NeurIPS 2026, v3 Oct 2026) are as stated in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law scaling of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No predictions from power-law fits on small runs are compared with much larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or scaling of that allocation with compute is tested.
No fixed-parameter-count comparison of depth, width, or architecture effects on loss is reported.
Fine-tuning performance is studied, but the paper does not test whether the same power-law form holds in fine-tuning or other regimes.
The paper predicts downstream fine-tuning metrics from short-run observations and configuration, not downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
No dependence of power-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices is measured.

rows.subject: LLM (model not stated)

rows.measure: Downstream LLM performance over training steps
rows.note: Text describes performance as improving with more training steps; this is not a power-law loss measurement.
rows.check: Downstream accuracy over fine-tuning steps for one configuration, figure only. It does not vary scale, so no version's effect can be read. The subject is likely Llama-3-8B-Instruct (the paper's main model) but Fig. 3 does not say so.

rows.operation_detail: Reports a fine-tuning performance trajectory for a suboptimal training configuration.
rows.measure: Downstream LLM performance over training steps
rows.note: Text says performance decreases as training steps increase for this configuration; it is downstream performance, not held-out loss.
rows.check: 'Reversed' has no referent because no version is linked. The row shows accuracy falling with more fine-tuning steps under a poor data mixture. That is a training-step trajectory at fixed model size, not a scaling relation.

rows.subject: JoBS performance predictor
rows.operation_detail: Measures predictor error as the number of full training runs used to train the predictor varies.

conditions.value: increasing number of initial full training runs

rows.note: The text reports higher R², tighter error concentration around zero, and decreasing error variance as N increases; no exact plotted values are stated.
rows.check: This measures the study's own method component: predictor R² and error as the number of predictor-training runs N grows. It should not be a result row on the claim. It is at most context for fits_no_version.
